title: Before you go.
summary: Practical notes to copy and adapt before an outing, school meeting or everyday plan. Clear questions, useful wording and details worth checking.

Copy it, edit it for your situation and keep personal information limited to what is useful. The practical detailsQuestions to ask and notes to borrow. Open whatever you need. Plan a day out Seven questions before you go A little more information before leaving the house can save a lot of guessing when you get there. When is it quieter?Ask about crowds, music, hand dryers, and scheduled events. Where can we take a break?Check for a calm space and whether you can leave and re-enter. What are the bathrooms like?Ask about privacy, space, and the specific facilities you need. What can we bring?Confirm food, drinks, communication devices, and familiar comfort items. How does the visit actually work?Check queues, parking distance, steps, seating, and any required waiting. Is the main attraction open?Confirm today's availability, hours, age rules, and access restrictions. What happens if plans change?Ask about cancellation, refunds, and a shorter visit before booking. ShareCopyPrint Ask for access A clear request can be short. Explain what gets in the way, say what would help, and ask for a reply in writing. A note you can borrow Hi, we're planning to visit [place] on [date]. A family member has a disability, and [barrier] makes it difficult to take part. Would it be possible to [specific adjustment]? Please let us know what you can arrange and who to ask for when we arrive. If that won't work, is there another option? A written reply would help us plan. Thank you! Copy this request Be specificCould we wait somewhere quieter until it's our turn?Could you send a few photos or tell us what happens during the visit?Can our support person stay with us?Could we have the instructions in writing too? You can begin with the access need. Your family's entire history needn't go into the first email. US guidance: businesses open to the public and effective communication. Duties and exceptions depend on the setting. This is a starting point for a request, not individual legal advice. Hotels and pools A lovely lobby is a bonus. A working pool and the right beds are rather more important. The room: what are the actual beds? Does the separate sleeping area have a door? “Suite” leaves a surprising amount unanswered.The pool: is it open on your dates? And the hot tub? Ask about hours, age rules, and water temperature if it matters to you.The timing: can you swim before check-in or after checkout?The food: what exactly is in the kitchenette? A fridge and microwave won't do the same job as a stove.The noise: ask about events, room location, and somewhere to take a quiet break.The bill: get the total with taxes, parking, fees, and deposits. Read the cancellation terms before paying. Hi, we're looking at a stay on [dates]. Could you confirm the beds and room layout, what's in the kitchenette, and whether both the indoor pool and hot tub will be open? We'd also like their hours and age rules, and whether we can use them before check-in or after checkout. Please include the total with mandatory fees, any deposit, and the cancellation terms. We also need [access adjustment]. Thanks so much! Copy the hotel questions Ask the property about your actual dates. An old pool photograph can only tell you so much. Support communication Please speak to the person. Give them time to answer. Those two things are a very good place to start. AAC means augmentative and alternative communication. Speech, vocalizations, gestures, signs, photographs, objects, writing, spelling, eye gaze, switches, low-tech boards and speech-generating devices can all be part of one multimodal system. Keep the person's communication method within reach. Ask before moving or touching a device.Leave time for a response before asking the question again.Offer choices the person can use, including “no,” “stop,” and “break.”Use language that respects their age. Speech alone doesn't tell you what someone understands. A note for a hostPlease speak directly to our family member and give them time to respond. They communicate using [method]. Please keep it available and ask before touching their device. It helps to [individual preference]. They may also need time to pause. Thank you for making room for this. Copy the communication note Read the full multimodal communication guide → Further reading: CommunicationFIRST, its guidance written by AAC users, and ASAN on autism. Understand ableism Ableism can show up in an ordinary exchange: talking over someone, dismissing an access request, or assuming a person won't enjoy an activity because they need help with it. Some autistic people need substantial support throughout their lives. They still have preferences, privacy, and every reason to be included. What that means hereInclude the person in the conversation.Speak to them, with the communication support they use.Allow a different sort of visit.A break, a shorter stay, or watching before joining in can make the day work.Keep support available.Comfort and communication shouldn't have to be earned.Let private moments stay private.A hard day doesn't need to become a public story. We write as a family. Autistic people speak for themselves, including through AAC, and their own words matter. ASAN on autism · CommunicationFIRST's wording guide If an access request is refused Ask for the reason in writing. It gives you something specific to respond to. Restate the barrier and the adjustment you asked for.Ask which policy applies, and whether another arrangement would work.Find out who can review the decision.Keep the dates and messages. Write down what happened while it's fresh. Thank you for getting back to us. The difficulty is [barrier], and we asked for [adjustment]. Could you explain why that isn't possible, share the relevant policy, and let us know whether an alternative would work? Who could review the request? We'd appreciate a written reply. Copy the follow-up For US rights guidance: businesses, government programs, and Massachusetts communication access. The rules depend on the setting; a refusal alone doesn't establish a legal violation. Make the day simpler One good thing is plentyPick the part of the day everyone is looking forward to. Leave space around it, and know what the shorter version looks like. Before the shoes go onConfirm the hours, parking, bathrooms, and food.Show what comes first, next, and afterward in a familiar way. Actual photos can help.Know where you can take a break, and how to get back to the car. For the bagA communication device and charger, familiar food and drink, a comfort item, spare clothes if needed, and the supplies in the person's usual support plan.There is no prize for staying longer than everyone wants to. Choices, routines & things to do Today's choices, pleaseA choice board needs to match what's actually available. For an ice-cream stop, that means today's flavors at the right shop.Offer a few clear choices, with words and useful pictures.Keep flavor, cone or cup, and size as separate decisions.A strawberry picture says more than a pink square.Include “something else,” “no,” and “finished.” Allow time to choose. A short plan for a new placeShow the place, who will be there, what happens, where a break can happen, and going home. Use real photos when you can. Leave room for things to change. Activities for teensStart with what interests them: swimming, animals, films, a walk, or making something to eat. The amount of help someone needs doesn't make their interests younger.Ask about group size, noise, pace, and whether a support person can join.Check the changing facilities and where to take a break.See whether a short introduction or trial visit is possible.Find a part of the activity they can choose and take part in, with the help they need. A note to hand overThe plan today is [activity and time]. Communication: [method and response time]. What helps: [specific support]. A break: [place or cue]. If plans change: [how to explain or contact us]. Please follow the existing support and emergency plans.Copy the handover note Share private care details securely with the people who need them. More on communication support. Clothes that feel right A beautiful sweater that nobody wants to wear is still a sweater sitting in a drawer.Start with the clothes that feel right. Then look at the details: the collar, the seams, the waistband, and whether the fastenings are manageable.Use measurements. One brand's medium isn't every brand's medium.Check washing and drying before buying.Build around a comfortable shape or color that already gets worn.Read the return policy, especially when ordering an unfamiliar fabric.Classic can be quite simple. Comfortable clothes, a useful layer, and no argument with the waistband.Build a useful wardrobe One family. Not the whole spectrum.We write about what we wear, where we go, what earns space in the house, and the practical side of life with profound autism. The point is not perfection. It is knowing enough to make a better choice before spending the money or loading the car.Our family experience includes profound autism and very high support needs. That gives us one specific lens - not ownership of autism, neurodiversity, or anybody else's story.What that means hereWe use profound autism descriptively for our family's support-needs reality. We know the term is contested. Some families and researchers find it useful; some autistic self-advocates strongly oppose it. We do not use it as a hierarchy of human worth.When we write generally, we usually use identity-first language such as autistic person, while respecting individual preferences when they are known. We welcome autistic and neurodivergent readers across support levels.Some details stay within our family. Useful does not require invasive.Read our language & representation standard Notes from New England A swim and a good lunchGive us somewhere to swim and something good to eat, and there is the beginning of a day out.It is tempting to add three more stops because they're nearby. They will still be there another day. Leave time to enjoy the thing you came for.Before leaving, check the opening hours, food, bathrooms, and somewhere to take a break. Keep a shorter version of the day in mind too.The questions to ask first The unglamorous questionsCan it go in the washing machine? Does the lid come apart for cleaning? Will it need a subscription after we've bought it?Those questions aren't much use in a beautiful photograph. They're rather useful once the parcel arrives.The same goes for meal kits. “Quick” can mean very different things once you count the chopping, extra ingredients, and washing up.The questions we ask before buying A shorter visitThere is a great deal of advice about making the most of a visit. Sometimes that means leaving while everyone is still having a good time.Watching for a while, doing one part, taking a break, or choosing to go home are all things a plan can allow for. Ask about re-entry before you need it.The person taking part should have a say in what comes next. title: Halloween, farm style.
summary: Skeleton glasses, corn sifting, a farm ride and memories of Connor’s Halloween Party at Frerichs Farm in Warren, Rhode Island.
search: The journalWarren, Rhode IslandA Halloween family field note Skeleton glasses. Cookie in hand. Not a bad way to start a Halloween story.A family afternoon at Frerichs FarmHalloween, farm style.A cookie, some spectacular skeleton glasses, corn to sift—and a farm that made a special Halloween invitation to autistic families.An AUsome Life · Published October 7, 2026 From an earlier family visitSome photographs bring back a whole afternoon. These are the ones with a yellow Black Panther shirt, a bit of Halloween mischief, and the three of us sitting close together in the October sunshine.They were taken at Frerichs Farm in Warren, Rhode Island. They still make me smile. Opened from the family albumA little skeleton and a lot of personality.The Halloween glasses deserve their own place in the album. White plastic bones frame a tiny skull, held up in front of one eye. A cookie is being kept very firmly in the other hand. The shirt is bright yellow, and absolutely none of the photograph looks like it needed organizing by an adult.Behind him, people are sitting under a big tent. The grass is green, the light is lovely, and it is the kind of unplanned photograph that ends up meaning more than the ones we spend ten minutes trying to pose.For us, these little moments are the story. Not how many attractions we did, or how much we fitted into an afternoon. Just the part we actually enjoyed. Pour, sift, watch, repeat. A good activity does not have to hurry.All three of us together in the autumn sun. A small activity, a real memoryThere was a table full of sand and corn.The sifting station was a wonderfully simple thing: a shallow tabletop, scattered corn kernels, a wooden screen, and a paper cup for pouring. It offered something to do with your hands and something interesting to watch happen.I love that we kept a picture of it. Sometimes the most absorbing stop of the day is not the grand attraction. It is an ordinary little activity that makes sense immediately, with no instructions required. A small study in autumn. Original editorial illustration.The invitation that matteredConnor’s Halloween Party.Frerichs Farm has hosted a special gathering called Connor’s Halloween Party, created for people on the autism spectrum and their families. It has been offered free of charge, with an RSVP, as a chance for families to enjoy some autumn fun together.That intention is part of why I wanted this farm in our family journal. A place can have pumpkins, wagons, treats and games, but there is something extra meaningful about an event that deliberately says to families like ours: this day is for you, too.Previous descriptions of the party mention activities such as the Western Town, pirate ship, bubbles, a scavenger hunt, a bouncy house and food. Activities can change by year, and a designated autism event is not a guarantee that every sound, surface or crowd will suit every person. Still, the invitation itself matters.A note on dates: Despite being a memory from an earlier visit, this is not necessarily a discontinued event. Frerichs Farm listed Connor’s Halloween for October 3, 2026 (rain date October 4). That date has passed; check the farm’s official party page and calendar for any future celebration and RSVP details. In the middle of it allThree of us, a patch of sun.We took several family selfies, and not one needed to be perfect. In one, our son looks away from the camera. In another, he turns toward us. The sun makes its own plans.We were there together. That is the picture I wanted to keep.The bright orange railings behind us, the blue jackets, the rows of white tents in the distance—those details make this feel like a specific day, not just a generic autumn outing.A second photograph from the same few sunny minutes. Little pieces of the dayThe camera kept rolling.There are a few short videos from the farm ride, too: a look at the tractor, an orange railing against the sky, and the happy disorder of everybody trying to get a view. I am keeping them here with the photographs, because sometimes a moving picture brings the whole place back. Ask about the route from parking to activities, wet-weather surfaces and any firm or step-free alternatives for strollers, wheelchairs and visitors who prefer steadier footing.Ask what the ride actually involves.If the tractor or pumpkin ride is operating, ask about loading, how long it lasts, how loud it may be, seating and whether someone can choose to watch instead. The photograph I come back to is still the one with the cookie and the skull glasses. There is no grand lesson in it. Just a child having an October afternoon his own way, and a place that thought about welcoming families who are not always included in the usual invitations.I'm glad we went. title: Get in the photograph.
summary: For the mother who plans the outing and takes the pictures: a reminder to get in the photograph, with a moment from our own family album.
search: Motherhood · From the family album Get in the photograph. For the mother who plans the outing, packs the bag, and takes the pictures: make sure there are some with you in them, too. October 16, 2026 Arms in the air. A moment from our family album. I love this one of James and me. Arms in the air, a grey New England sky, a little silliness beside the water. This is part of motherhood I want to remember: enjoying each other’s company. Hand someone the phone. Ask for a few pictures. You don’t have to arrange everyone, put away the familiar things, or wait for matching smiles. Leave room for the moment as it is. And when you look through them, give yourself a little kindness. Keep the one that makes you remember being there together. You belong in the family album. Explore related topicsThe journal / Family life Self-care Self-care & relationships

title: A grocery run, then breakfast by the water.
summary: A Saturday Hannaford stop during our off-season trip to Wells, Maine: Oakhurst eggnog cold brew, our own plates and glasses, and breakfast at a waterside picnic table.
search: Hannaford · Our off-season Wells tripA grocery run, then breakfast by the water.Oakhurst eggnog cold brew, our own plates and glasses, and a waterside picnic table. A simple Saturday breakfast idea from our Maine getaway, with a grocery stop James was very happy to make.October 18, 2026 · From the family notebook The makings of breakfast on our Wells trip, before we found our table by the water. On our trip to Wells, a quick Saturday morning stop at Hannaford became breakfast at a picnic table by the water. We had brought our own glasses and plates, so our grocery-store breakfast got a proper little table setting. I’ve loved Hannaford for years. I lived in Vermont for a long time, and it is one of those familiar places I’m always pleased to see when we’re away. I was hoping for my favorite butter rum muffins. They were sold out, which was a small disappointment, but we found plenty else to enjoy. We picked up assorted muffins, chocolate-frosted donuts, cold brew and Oakhurst eggnog. The eggnog added a Maine connection of its own: Oakhurst is a longtime Portland dairy. At our waterside table, we mixed eggnog into the cold brew and made our own eggnog coffee drinks. James had his eggnog on its own. It’s never off-season for eggnog. James had a good morning in the aisles, too. James loves grocery shopping. He was enjoying himself so much that other shoppers commented, and we proudly shared that he is often the grocery-store trip leader in his classroom. Shopping is one of his favorite things to do, and it was lovely to have a chance to tell people about that part of his school day. Then it was breakfast by the water: muffins, donuts, our little cold-brew experiment and time to sit together. We enjoyed it so much that we forgot to take a waterfront photo. The butter rum muffins can stay on the list for next time. Original editorial illustration, inspired by breakfast during our off-season Wells trip. A small idea to borrowBring the table setting. We found a waterside table and settled in with our breakfast. title: A date at the Gardner.
summary: A date at Boston’s Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, with our own photograph, practical caregiver planning, admission savings and museum accessibility notes.
search: Boston, Massachusetts · Time for two A date at the Gardner. A beautiful place, a little time together, and a photograph of just the two of us. There is room for this part of family life, too. October 16, 2026 · From our family album Just the two of us at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston. There is a place in our family album for just the two of us. Here we are at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, tucked beside a stone column, with that extraordinary courtyard behind us. A little Boston date, worth keeping. So much of family life happens in conversation about what needs doing next. The calendar, the ride, the groceries, the things that need remembering. I like having a photograph that holds something else: us, together, somewhere beautiful. The Gardner makes a lovely setting for that sort of outing. The courtyard gives you something to pause over before you have made a single decision about which room to see. Its plant displays change through the seasons; the museum’s own courtyard guide is a good place to see what might be there on a future visit. A museum date can be wonderfully modest. Choose a few rooms. Point out a detail you like. Ask which painting your partner would take home if such things were permitted. Leave enough time to enjoy being there without making the entire collection an assignment. Time together belongs in the family calendar. Make the date small enough to happen. For parents and caregivers, getting out together can take real arranging. Reliable help, money and a workable window of time all matter. When those pieces are available, a short date deserves a place in the plan. An hour or two can be a perfectly good beginning. Before booking, agree who is covering care, the return time, and how to reach you if needed. Put the essential information in one place; our caregiver handover guide can help. Build in the journey home so the last room does not become a race against the clock. Choose one main stop and let anything else be optional. The museum lists Café G for food and coffee; check its arrangements separately if you want to add it. Leaving after the museum is also a complete date. And if a museum visit is beyond this week’s budget or support arrangements, keep the idea of time together in a smaller form: a cup of tea after the house settles, a shared album, a few minutes talking about something you are both looking forward to. The people doing the caring belong in the picture, too. The practical details left inBefore your own Boston date. Tickets, timing & a less expensive dateThe museum is at 25 Evans Way, Boston. Advance timed tickets are recommended. Standard adult admission is currently $25; ages 17 and under enter free. It is closed Tuesdays. Check current hours and availability on the official visit page.Thursday evenings are free, 5–9 p.m. Registration opens Tuesday at 10 a.m., two days beforehand; walk-up admission is not guaranteed. Use the Free Thursday Nights page to book. Participating library passes offer $5 admission for up to four adults; you must reserve the pass and obtain timed tickets with its code. A free evening may be busy, so choose the timing that suits you. Mobility, seating & sensory considerationsThe museum reports elevators in both buildings and a Palace lift to bypass the two steps before its main elevator. Free loan wheelchairs, rollators and canes are limited and first come, first served. Historic rooms have varied flooring, narrow doorways and low lighting; some power chairs may not fit every doorway.Gallery benches are available, with fewer on the upper Palace floors. Public restrooms have accessible stalls. These are the museum’s published provisions; we have not tested each route or facility. For individual access questions, call 617-278-5156 and review the accessibility guide. Ask about a quieter visiting time if crowds or sound affect your plans. Arrival & parkingThe museum has no dedicated visitor parking lot. Its directions page lists nearby options, including discounted Simmons garage parking with museum validation. title: A Little Heat on Cape Cod: Dinner at Kohinoor
summary: A recommendation from a local artist led us to excellent Indian food in Mashpee—and a restaurant where our son was made to feel entirely welcome.
search: Kohinoor · Mashpee, MassachusettsA Little Heat on Cape Cod: Dinner at KohinoorA recommendation from a local artist led us to excellent Indian food in Mashpee—and a restaurant where our son was made to feel entirely welcome.By Michael, James’s dad · October 25, 2026James’s picture choice board ↓ James at Kohinoor in Mashpee. First things first: Kohinoor served us the best Indian food we’ve ever eaten. We love Indian food, we have eaten plenty of it, and we have opinions. This meal did nothing to make us less opinionated. We found the place through Laura DiMeo, the artist behind Perch Pottery in East Falmouth. We had reached out about visiting her studio, and she graciously welcomed our family for what became nearly two hours of conversation and a personal tour. Meeting an artist where she works is a pleasure in itself. Laura was also a delightful host. When the conversation turned to our fondness for Indian cuisine, she recommended Kohinoor Indian Restaurant & Bar in nearby Mashpee. We took her advice. Our order was entirely vegetarian: samosa chaat, aloo gobi, palak paneer, and garlic naan. We also happen to love heat. Serious heat. The kitchen had no difficulty accommodating us. The food The samosa chaat was an excellent introduction. Pieces of samosa mingled with chickpeas, onions, and tangy peppers; sweetness, bitterness, spice, and crunch kept turning up in different combinations. There was a lot going on, and every part of it seemed to belong there. Next came the aloo gobi. We ordered the potatoes and cauliflower very spicy, and the kitchen took us seriously. Very seriously. The impressive thing was how much flavor survived all that heat. Both vegetables were cooked perfectly and retained their individual textures. You could still taste the potatoes, the cauliflower, and the spices. The heat gave the whole thing considerable force without flattening everything beneath it. Making food hot is one thing. Making it this good at that level of heat takes some care. The palak paneer was equally convincing. Fresh-tasting spinach, soft paneer, and a rich, creamy sauce with enough heat to keep things interesting (yes, we ordered this one spicy, too). The creaminess and spice worked beautifully together. Nothing seemed to be compensating for anything else. And the garlic naan: fragrant, flavorful, crisp in places and gently chewy in others. An excellent companion to the curries, though it hardly needed their help. Not a single dish disappointed us. At the table with James Our teenage son, James, has significant support needs. He also likes going out with his family. We like finding places where all three of us can enjoy a meal without spending much of it explaining ourselves. My wife photographed the menu and used ChatGPT to make a choice board: eight options with pictures James could point to. He has his own opinions about dinner; the pictures give him another way to make them known. The choice board made for James from Kohinoor’s menu. The food pictures are AI-generated illustrations, not photographs of the restaurant’s dishes. Download James’s choice board (PNG)An independent picture resource based on the menu during our visit. Check current choices with your server, and keep familiar ways to say no, ask for help, or choose something else available.The staff were entirely comfortable with James. More than that, they seemed to get a kick out of him. Their warmth was easy and unforced, and they were attentive to the practical things. They brought his drinks in plastic cups with lids, a small but thoughtful detail that made the meal easier. When we requested a plastic spoon, one appeared almost immediately. None of this became an undertaking. The drinks arrived in cups that worked for him; we asked for a spoon and got one. That sort of straightforward attention goes a long way. As James’s dad, I am fairly alert to the difference between a restaurant tolerating our presence and actually enjoying having us there. Kohinoor gave us every reason to believe it was the latter. James was another guest, with a family and an appetite. No awkwardness required. The restaurant itself was immaculate: soft green walls, warm pendant lighting, floral accents, and comfortable booths. Even the small details—the patterned pots and white blooms—were worth a look. The service was impeccable throughout. A few of the small details: white blooms, patterned pots, and green walls. Worth the return trip I could recommend Kohinoor on the aloo gobi alone. The palak paneer, samosa chaat, and garlic naan make that recommendation considerably easier. So does a staff who made having dinner with our son feel as ordinary and enjoyable as it ought to. We went in hoping for a good Indian meal. We came out revising our list of favorites. Thank you, Laura, for the recommendation. And thank you, Kohinoor, for looking after us so well. We’ll be back. title: Words matter. So does context.
summary: How An AUsome Life approaches autism, disability, high-support needs and respectful representation.
search: Editorial standardWords matter. So does context.An AUsome Life uses clear, respectful language and avoids turning disability into either tragedy or inspiration content.Identity-first by defaultWe usually use “autistic person” rather than “person with autism,” while respecting an individual’s own preference when known.High-support / profoundWe use high-support language when it helps explain access needs. “Profound autism” may appear when discussing the specific high-support experience this publication covers; we do not present the term as universally preferred or as a hierarchy of human value.No pity framingSupport needs can be significant without making a disabled person a tragedy, lesson or campaign prop.Age-respectful alwaysTeenagers remain teenagers. We do not infantilize someone because their communication, learning or daily-living support needs are substantial.For brandsWe will not use cure/fixing language, staged distress, forced participation or intimate private details to make a story more emotional. Product claims must stay within responsible evidence.
